content: Potassium sodium tartrate is a double salt that was first synthesized around the year 1675 by Pierre Seignette, an apothecary from La Rochelle, France. Due to its origin, the compound became known as Seignette's salt or Rochelle salt. It appears as a colorless to blue-white crystalline substance that crystallizes in the orthorhombic system. Its molecular formula is KNaC₄H₄O₆·4H₂O. This compound is only slightly soluble in alcohol but dissolves more readily in water. It has a melting point of approximately 75°C and exhibits a saline, cooling taste. As a food additive, it is identified by the E number E337. Historically, it has been used medicinally as a purgative. However, in more recent years, its piezoelectric properties have gained prominence, leading to its application in devices such as phonograph pickups and other sensing equipment. Rochelle salt has also been utilized in the silvering process of mirrors. It is a key component of Fehling's solution, which was previously employed to detect reducing sugars in solutions. In organic synthesis, it is used during aqueous workups to break emulsions, particularly in reactions involving aluminum-based hydride reagents. Rochelle salt can be synthesized from common household items such as cream of tartar and washing soda or baking powder. Due to its significant temperature-dependent solubility, large crystals of Rochelle salt can be easily grown. Additionally, it is an ingredient in the Biuret reagent, which is used to measure protein concentration.
